Keywords: medical image segmentation, uncertainty estimation, deep learning, nnUNet, temperature scaling, deep ensembles, checkpoint ensembles, test-time augmentation, en-tropy visualization, CT iii Abstract in lingua italiana Negli ultimi anni, il deep learning ha dimostrato prestazioni straordinarie nei compiti di segmentazione di immagini mediche. Research Objectives The overarching goal of this thesis is to investigate, implement, and evaluate techniques for uncertainty estimation in deep learning-based medical image segmentation. These include post-hoc calibration through temperature scaling, the use of deep ensembles to capture variability across independently trained models, test-time augmentation to probe input-dependent uncertainty, and checkpoint-based posterior sampling to approximate Bayesian inference over training dynamics. The models are evaluated not only in terms of their segmentation accuracy—measured via Dice Similarity Coefficient—but also based on the quality of their uncertainty estimates, using metrics such as Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier Score. 59 5.2 Comparison of predictive uncertainty maps and segmentation results across three anatomical planes (coronal, sagittal, axial) for six different methods.

results.title: A literature review of artificial intelligence (AI) for medical image segmentation: from AI and explainable AI to trustworthy AI - PMC
results.content: Chen *et al.* (47) innovatively incorporated a transformer model into medical image segmentation and created the TransUNet. This model efficiently encodes robust global contexts by treating image features as sequences, and integrates low-layer CNN features through a U-shaped hybrid design, synergizing the strengths of both the transformer and U-Net (*Figure 2B*). Chen *et al.* (99) proposed a new causal CAM (C-CAM) method to solve the problem of unclear foreground-background boundaries and serious co-occurrence in the weakly supervised semantic segmentation of medical images (*Figure 11B*). Kaur *et al.* (111) proposed an XAI-based medical image segmentation model, GradXcepUNet, which combines the segmentation capability of the U-Net with the interpretability feature of Grad-CAM’s Xception classification network. Ghnemat *et al.* (113) introduced an XAI model for medical image classification to enhance the interpretability of decision-making processes. Future research directions include exploring new AI architectures, integrating multimodal data fusion techniques, and advancing TAI methods to improve the reliability and trustworthiness of AI in medical image segmentation.
